q: You want to anchor overnight off this coast to wait for a fair stream. The best depth for your chain lies inside the box. What do you do?
answer: Anchor elsewhere — not in a dumping ground
why: A disused explosives dumping ground may still hold live munitions: never anchor, trawl or dive there.

q: Your night track passes 0.2 M from this offshore buoy, and AIS shows a tanker heading for it. What do you do?
answer: Re-route well clear — a tanker moors, hoses float
why: A single buoy mooring holds a loading tanker and floating hoses; 0.2 M is 370 m, inside the 500 m area: keep well off.

q: Your track crosses this charted symbol, and later you plan to anchor near it to wait for the stream. What do you do?
answer: Cross it, but anchor well away from it
why: A suspended wellhead stands on the seabed, here 14 m down: no danger to your keel, but anchors and nets snag on it.

q: Making a night landfall, this bearing of the light ahead is your only position line. What does it give you?
answer: Whether you are on track, not how far to go
why: A bearing along your track checks the cross-track error only; distance to go needs a line that cuts across it.

q: Northbound across the Bay, the sounder first finds the bottom at 190 m at 0420. Which part of your DR does this check?
answer: The distance run — the edge lies across the track
why: A contour is a position line; this one cuts your track at right angles, so it checks the distance run (log and along-track stream).

q: At 20 kn at night you want a three-light fix with the hand-bearing compass. In which order do you take the bearings?
answer: A, C, then B
why: Take the lights ahead and astern first — their bearings change slowly — and B, nearest the beam, last; then note the time and log.

q: You are on this bearing of the light; the sounder reads below its transducer. Where on the line are you?
answer: B — at the 43 m sounding
why: Charted depth = sounding 45.0 + transducer 1.0 − tide 3.0 = 43.0 m, so you are at B.

q: The radar ranges of the two islands cross at X and Y. Which is your position?
answer: X — the rough bearing of A fits only X
why: From X, island A bears about 333°T; from Y it would bear 290°T. Even a rough EBL tells the two crossings apart.

q: Northbound in fog over the shelf, you log these soundings every 2 M. Which track have you been on?
answer: Track B
why: Only on B does the canyon fall on the third sounding: 142, 148, then 405 m, then back to 155 and 160 m.

figure.note: Soundings every 2 M, from the south

q: You have this single bearing of the light and a good sounding. How much does the sounding add?
answer: Little — the depth hardly changes along the line
why: The contours run along this bearing, so the depth is about 84 m all along it; a sounding helps only where contours cross the line.

q: Your only position line is this bearing of the light, and your EP lies off it. Where on the line do you put yourself?
answer: At the point on it nearest the EP
why: With one line and an EP, take the point on the line nearest the EP: the smallest shift that fits both.

q: Your track was laid 2 M off this wind farm. At night you find yourself 1.5 M off the track towards it. What do you do?
answer: Regain the track: it holds the planned margin
why: The track was set for a 2 M margin; a new course for B from here keeps you nearer the farm. Get back on the line.

q: With no stream offshore you find yourself off the track, as shown. How much do you alter to head straight for B?
answer: 10° to starboard
why: 1 in 60: 5 M over the 75 M run is 4° of track error; 5 M over the 50 M to go is 6° more to close: 10° in all.

q: Your sister yacht, 30 M due east, must transfer an injured crew member to you and holds her course. Which course do you steer to meet her soonest?
why: Collision course: sin A = 6 × sin 90° ÷ 8, A = 49° off her bearing towards her course: 090° + 49° = 139°T. 127°T aims where she is in 3 h 45.

q: At night in the north-east-bound lane, the plotter shows you set towards the separation zone, with the bend ahead. What do you do?
answer: Regain the lane's track and follow it round the bend
why: In a lane a new course to the waypoint cuts the corner through the separation zone; get back on the planned track.

figure.note: Night · XTE 0.6 M towards the zone · sketch

ru.Night · XTE 0.6 M towards the zone · ske: Ночь · XTE 0,6 мили к зоне · схема

q: You want to strike the coast 6 M north of the harbour, with this current across your track all the way. Which heading do you steer?
why: The current sets you 12 M north in 20 h; you want only 6 M: 6 M to cancel, 6 × 60 ÷ 120 = 3° south of 090°T, 093°T.

q: You are passing Portland Bill on the E-going spring stream. Where does the race lie now?
answer: East and SE of the Bill, downstream
why: A race forms where the stream sweeps past the headland and spreads downstream: on the E-going stream, E and SE of the Bill.

q: Your 24 m motor yacht is crossing an offshore bank at 18 kn with a swell running. What do you have under the keel in the troughs?
why: 6.2 m charted + 1.0 m tide = 7.2 m; less half the 2.0 m swell, 0.4 m of squat and the 2.4 m draught: 3.4 m in the troughs.

q: You are closing this point at night, and your plan offers three clearing bearings on the light. Which do you use?
answer: C — the 10 m line, for the draught in a swell
why: On the 5 m line a 3 m swell takes 1.5 m off your 1.6 m: almost nothing. At night with a deep draught, clear the 10 m line.

q: Your night route north must get past the end of this scheme. Which crossing do you plan?
answer: A — across both lanes at right angles
why: Ships converge and turn in a precautionary area, with no set direction; a right-angle crossing of the lanes meets predictable traffic.

figure.note: Ships converge and turn in the area

ru.Ships converge and turn in the area: Суда сходятся и поворачивают в районе

q: You must anchor in this unlit bay tonight. How do you find the planned spot?
answer: By two radar ranges off the steep points, checked by the sounder
why: Ranges off steep points are the sharpest radar fix in the dark; the sounder confirms the depth. Bearings smear by the beam width.

figure.note: Depths in metres; dashed arcs: ranges

q: Fog closes in as you round this cliff on radar. Outside what VRM ring do you keep the cliff’s echo?
why: The low reef gives no echo, so measure from the cliff: 0.7 M of reef + 0.5 M margin = keep the cliff outside 1.2 M.

figure.note: Plan: round the cliff, reef to starboard

q: Checking tonight’s route, you find WP4 here. What do you do?
answer: Move it clear of the point where the ships turn
why: Ships converge and alter at the same point off a cape; a yacht turning there meets them all, mid-turn. Put WP4 clear of their routes.

figure.note: Ship routes from the routeing guide

ru.Ship routes from the routeing guide: Пути судов — по руководству по путям

q: You plot this echo on the night watch. If neither of you alters, when does she reach you?
answer: About 0248
why: Steady bearing, CPA nil: 2.0 M closed in 12 min = 10 kn, so the 6.0 M left take 36 min from 0212 → 0248.

q: The third plot of this echo falls off the line of the first two. What CPA does she now give?
answer: CPA 2.1 M at 0525
why: The bend at 0506 shows she has altered: plot afresh from 0506 and 0512 only. That line passes 2.1 M off, CPA at 0525.

q: This yacht’s echo appears 2 M off, and the guard zone never sounded. Why not?
answer: Her echo first showed inside the zone’s inner edge
why: A small echo may first paint at 2–3 M; a ring from 6 M out never sees it. A guard zone helps the lookout, it does not replace one.

q: A ship passes close and the radar paints this arc around her. What is it?
answer: Side lobes from her strong echo, not real targets
why: A big echo close by returns energy through the scanner’s side lobes, painting an arc at her range. Turn the gain or sea clutter down a touch.

q: Your passage runs past this traffic separation scheme without using it. How do you plan the route?
answer: Keep clear of it by as wide a margin as you can
why: Rule 10(h): a vessel not using a scheme avoids it by as wide a margin as practicable; 10(f), (g): care near its ends, no anchoring.

q: You are bound along this coast, past the scheme. May you use the inshore traffic zone?
answer: No — at 22 m under power you must use the lane
why: Rule 10(d): the inshore zone is for vessels under 20 m, sailing and fishing vessels, or to reach a place in it — not a 22 m motor yacht passing by.

q: Your 22 m motor yacht is bound for Port A, inside this inshore traffic zone. May you leave the lane and use the zone to get there?
answer: Yes — you are bound for a port within the zone
why: Rule 10(d)(ii): any vessel may use an inshore traffic zone when en route to or from a port, installation or place situated within it.

q: You must cross this scheme to the north under sail, but the wind blows straight down the right-angle heading. What do you do?
answer: Motor-sail across on a heading of 000°T
why: Rule 10(c): cross on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the flow — with an engine aboard, 000°T is practicable.

q: You are sailing east along this lane at night in your 22 m sloop. Where in the lane do you keep?
answer: Near its outer edge, well clear of the zone
why: Rule 10(b)(ii): keep clear of a separation line or zone; near the outer edge you also impede the ships least (10(j)).

q: You are heading E onto the continental shelf with this forecast. Where on the route will the gale's sea be worst?
answer: At B — over the shelf edge
why: Where the bottom rises from ocean depths to 200 m the waves steepen and turn confused: cross the shelf edge before a gale.

q: You read this analysis, with a secondary low south of the main one, before choosing your track. At which point do you expect the strongest wind?
answer: B — on the far side of the secondary
why: On the side of a secondary away from the main low the two circulations add: the strongest wind. Between the two centres they oppose.

q: You are heading east at 6 kn at night, and the radar shows this cell crossing ahead of you. What do you do?
answer: Slow down, let it cross, pass astern of it
why: Treat a moving cell like a ship crossing at 18 kn: you cannot outpace it, so slow down, let it cross, then pass behind it.

figure.note: Radar, 2300 · cell moving S at 18 kn

ru.Radar, 2300 · cell moving S at 18 kn: Радар, 2300 · ячейка идёт на S, 18 уз

q: The yard will haul you on their slipway today. At what state of the tide do you motor onto the submerged cradle?
answer: On the last of the flood, about an hour before HW
why: Come on with the tide still rising: if she is badly placed, the flood lifts her clear to try again. On the ebb she can be left on it askew.

figure.note: Cradle hauled up the rails by winch

q: You have touched on this bank and will lay the kedge out into deep water with the tender. How do you do it?
answer: Anchor and warp in the tender, warp paid out as you go
why: Pay the warp out from the tender as you go, so you never drag its weight through the water; drop the anchor at full length.

q: Your 22 m motor yacht is pinned to this quay with a yacht close ahead. You want to leave bow first. How do you get the bow out?
answer: Stern spring on, fender aft, port engine astern
why: Going astern on the stern spring holds the quarter and swings the bow out; the outboard (port) engine astern adds to it.

figure.note: Twin screws · wind E 5, onto the quay

ru.Twin screws · wind E 5, onto the quay: Два винта · ветер E 5 баллов, на причал

q: You are going astern into this slot from rest. What will she try to do, and how do you counter it?
answer: Bow falls to starboard; thruster to port, sternway early
why: A right-handed prop kicks the stern to port going astern, and the wind on the port beam blows the bow to starboard: both turn her one way.

figure.note: 20 m sloop, one RH prop · wind W 5

ru.20 m sloop, one RH prop · wind W 5: Шлюп 20 м, один правый винт · ветер W 5

q: You are to moor fore-and-aft between these two piles in a Solent river. How do you make the approach?
answer: Head west into the ebb; bow line to the west pile first
why: Stem the stream for control, make the bow fast to the up-tide pile first, then drop back on it and take the stern line to the other.

figure.note: Fore-and-aft between piles · ebb 2 kn E

ru.Fore-and-aft between piles · ebb 2 kn E: Между сваями · отлив 2 уз на E

q: You are towing this yacht towards the harbour entrance over the bar. What do you do before you reach it?
answer: Shorten the tow, for control and to keep the bight off the bottom
why: A long catenary can drag on a shallow bar and gives no control in a narrow entrance; shorten up in sheltered water, then go alongside.

q: You will lay a Bahamian moor here, stemming the flood, with 40 m of chain on each anchor. How do you lay it?
answer: First anchor, drop back 80 m, second anchor, heave back to the middle
why: Let go the up-stream anchor, drop back twice the scope, let go the second, then heave in on the first: she lies midway, 40 m to each.

figure.note: Bahamian moor · 40 m of chain on each

q: You ran onto this bank on the falling tide, and the wind is pushing her further onto it. When do you lay out the kedge?
answer: Now, into deep water to windward, taking up slack as she lifts
why: As she lifts the wind will drive her further up the bank; a kedge laid to windward now holds her, and you heave in as the tide comes.

q: You are stemming this stream in your 23 m twin-screw yacht, stopped over the ground 5 m off your gap on the quay. How do you close the last 5 m?
answer: Both ahead to hold the stream, bow angled in a little
why: Split engines give little or no thrust ahead, so the stream carries her back; held on both engines, bow angled in, the stream ferries her across.

figure.note: Twin screws · stopped over the ground, 5 m off

ru.Twin screws · stopped over the ground, 5: Два винта · без хода, в 5 м от места

q: You are heading downstream to this berth on the quay, and the river is too narrow to turn your 23 m twin-screw yacht. How do you come alongside?
answer: Pass the berth, stop, then back up to it against the stream
why: Going astern into the stream she is stemming it, slow over the ground and under control; with the stream behind her she cannot stop.

figure.note: River 1.2 lengths wide · 23 m, twin screws

ru.River 1.2 lengths wide · 23 m, twin scre: Река шириной 1,2 корпуса · 23 м, два винта
